name: Abdominal etching (high-definition lipo)

lead: Abdominal etching uses liposuction to remove fat in specific patterns so the abdominal muscle lines show more clearly. It was first described in 1993 and later extended to high-definition liposculpture with ultrasound-assisted devices.
It is mostly sought by lean, muscular people. Evidence consists of surgeon case series and one systematic review.

paras: Fat is suctioned at variable depths, including superficial layers, along muscle landmarks such as the linea alba and tendinous intersections. Some versions add fat transfer into the muscle area.
Reported risks include contour irregularities, asymmetry, umbilical changes, infection and bleeding, plus the general risks of liposuction.

lead: Abdominal etching is a liposuction technique that removes fat at variable depths and in superficial layers to emphasize the lines of the abdominal muscles, giving the appearance of a defined abdomen or 'six-pack'. It was first described in the early 1990s and was later extended into high-definition liposculpture using VASER ultrasound technology.[1][2][3]

It is sought mainly by people with a lean body and developed musculature who report not achieving the look through diet and exercise alone.[2][4] Reviews describe published outcomes mostly as surgeon case series, and complications and patient selection have been discussed in the literature.[4][5]
infobox: Lean patients, mostly male in early reports

paras: A 1993 paper in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery introduced abdominal etching, describing differential liposuction that targets landmarks including the linea alba, the linea semilunaris and the transverse tendinous intersections of the rectus abdominis.[2] A 1997 article revisited the technique, and a 2019 history review discussed its past and present.[6][7]

A 2007 report described VASER-assisted high-definition liposculpture, noting that ultrasound-based technology allowed liposuction of the superficial fat layers and that earlier differential lipoplasty had been limited to small areas in lean male patients.[1] Wikipedia also lists abdominal etching among liposuction variants first described in 1993.[8]

The etching technique is performed with liposuction in a superficial plane to create indentations that correspond to muscle landmarks.[4] Later variants combine liposuction with fat transfer, including ultrasound-guided fat grafting into the rectus abdominis muscle to increase apparent muscle volume.[3] A 2021 report addressed umbilical sagging after medium-definition liposuction.[9]

Complications reported for liposuction generally apply, including contour irregularities, asymmetry, infection, bleeding and, rarely, serious events.[8] The superficial plane used in etching is associated in the literature with higher risk of contour problems than deeper liposuction.[1][4]

A 2022 systematic review examined surgical techniques and outcomes of high-definition lipoplasty in male patients.[5] A 2019 report in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery described one surgeon's technique and outcomes, and a 2020 chapter in Clinics in Plastic Surgery reviewed the procedure.[4][10] No randomized controlled trials were identified; the evidence is largely surgeon-reported case series.
